films.name: Pan 100

grainStructure.value: Conventional cubic grain, similar in structure to Ilford's films but with a slightly softer, more old-fashioned curve.

origin.note: Kentmere is Harman Technology's budget brand, made in the same factory as Ilford film but to its own specification. It is not simply repackaged FP4 or HP5.

films.history: Kentmere was a Cumbrian photographic paper maker that Harman Technology bought in 2008, and the brand was relaunched for a budget black-and-white film range coated at Mobberley. Kentmere Pan 100 is the slow version: a traditional cubic emulsion with a soft curve and a very reasonable price. It is aimed at students and at anyone who wants to shoot a lot of black and white without worrying about the cost per frame.

characteristics.label: Price
characteristics.value: One of the cheapest first-party B&W films in Europe.

characteristics.label: Look
characteristics.value: Softer and slightly flatter than FP4 Plus, with more forgiving highlights.

films.name: Pan 400

grainStructure.value: Conventional cubic grain, visibly coarser than HP5's at the same speed.

origin.note: Harman's budget brand, coated alongside the Ilford films but to its own recipe.

films.history: Kentmere Pan 400 is the fast member of Harman's budget range, and it is the cheapest way to shoot a British 400-speed film. It is grainier and a little softer than HP5 Plus, and it pushes less gracefully. For street work and experimentation it is excellent value; for anything precious, most people reach for HP5.

characteristics.label: Push
characteristics.value: To EI 800 with a visible contrast and grain penalty; not a dedicated push film.

characteristics.label: Price
characteristics.value: The cheapest 400-speed film from a major European plant.

films.name: Ortho Plus

grainStructure.value: Fine cubic grain in an orthochromatic emulsion: sensitive to blue and green, blind to red.

films.history: Ilford Ortho Plus is a sheet-film orthochromatic material, ISO 80, intended for copy work, scientific photography and darkroom use where red-blindness is the point. It can be handled under a red safelight, renders lips and red objects black, and gives the tonality of early twentieth-century portraiture. Ilford still coats it in 4×5 and 8×10.

characteristics.label: Safelight
characteristics.value: Orthochromatic, so a dim red safelight is safe during handling.

characteristics.label: Rendering
characteristics.value: Red goes black, blue goes white. The classic period look.

characteristics.label: Use
characteristics.value: Copy work, alt processes and portraits with a 19th-century feel.

films.name: Pan F

grainStructure.value: Very fine conventional grain, the original 1950s ultra-fine emulsion.

films.history: Pan F was Ilford's slow film from the late 1950s until Pan F Plus replaced it in 1990. It was the standard fine-grain film of the 1960s and 1970s, and its tonality is slightly different from the Plus — softer in the midtones and with a longer toe. Expired rolls still turn up and develop surprisingly well.

characteristics.label: Difference from Plus
characteristics.value: Softer midtones and a longer toe; the Plus is contrastier and finer.

films.name: HP5

grainStructure.value: The original 1976 cubic emulsion, coarser and less controlled than the Plus that replaced it.

films.history: HP5 was Ilford's first high-speed film, introduced in 1976 and replaced by HP5 Plus in 1989. It was the film of British photojournalism in the late 1970s, grainier and a little less sharp than its successor, with a soft shoulder that held highlights. Any surviving stock is now decades expired.

characteristics.label: Expired stock
characteristics.value: Add about a stop per two decades and develop with a restrainer.

films.name: FP4

grainStructure.value: Conventional cubic grain, the classic 1968 fine-grain structure.

films.history: FP4 was 'Fine grain Panchromatic' from 1968, and it was the standard British medium-speed film for two decades. FP4 Plus replaced it in 1990 with a sharper, cleaner emulsion. Expired FP4 is common in old cameras and is usually still usable, if a little fogged.

characteristics.label: Look
characteristics.value: Soft and slightly flat compared with FP4 Plus, with a long toe.

films.name: XP1

grainStructure.value: Chromogenic dye-cloud grain, the first generation of Ilford's C-41 monochrome films.

films.history: XP1 was Ilford's first chromogenic black-and-white film, introduced in the early 1980s and developed in C-41. It was a revelation at the time: a black-and-white film that any minilab could process. XP2 replaced it in the 1990s. Its grain is softer and its contrast lower than XP2 Super's.
